dimensions.detail: spans 2011-01-08 to 2012-12-31 (723 days); sorted; 0 unparseable timestamps
no identifier-like text columns among features

quality.note: Scores describe the data as published. Nothing here is repaired at the ingestion layer; remediation happens inside the modelling pipeline where it can be fitted per-fold.

gaps.policy: The archive omits 165 hours. They are reindexed in as explicit NaNs rather than left as absent rows, so a 24-lag is genuinely 24 hours back. Rows whose target is missing are excluded from training and scoring; they are never imputed, because inventing demand would corrupt both the lag features and the error metric.
gaps.warmup_reason: The 168-hour look-back is undefined at the start of the series; those rows cannot be scored fairly.
gaps.forbidden_reason: casual + registered == cnt exactly. Either would give a perfect score and neither is known before the hour happens.

decomposition.note: STL with a 24-hour period. The seasonal share tells you how much of demand is pure daily rhythm -- and therefore how much a model can possibly add beyond knowing the hour.

correlogram.note: Peaks at lag 24 and 168 are what motivated those lags as features: yesterday's same hour and last week's same hour carry the most information in a commuting series.

stationarity.interpretation: ADF and KPSS test opposite nulls, so they are only convincing when they agree. Hourly bike demand is strongly seasonal rather than trending: the level is stable but the daily cycle is enormous, which is why the models here use explicit seasonal lags rather than differencing.
